extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students (practitioners in patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules governing who may be plaintiffs or defendants in equity actions for patent infringement, how and when parties must be joined or may be added, the capacity in which suits must be brought, and related doctrines (misjoinder, nonjoinder, conveyances pendente lite, collusive suits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief limited to infringements within district
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs are entitled to a decree for an accounting in respect of all infringements committed in this district by making or using or vending therein, and to an injunction against making in this district, and against using therein, and against vending therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiffs desire an accounting and injunction for infringements in another district they must proceed by a bill filed there. Examples/cases cited (e.g., Bobbie v. Smith) illustrate territorial limitations and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suits may be maintained against resident defendants despite acts beyond district
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit may be maintained against a defendant in the district of his residence, though the infringing acts to be enjoined or compensated for would be or were committed beyond its territorial limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity has jurisdiction to enforce its decrees against a resident in the district wherever the infringement was committed; cited cases include Hatch v. Hall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties to a suit in equity — who must be made parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The parties to a suit in equity comprise all those persons, natural or artificial, who can be affected by the decree, without regard to their number or the diversity of their relations to the subject-matter of the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any person having, at the time of the infringement, either a legal or an equitable interest in the patented invention which has been or is capable of being prejudiced by the infringing act may be a party plaintiff. If no party plaintiff has a legal or equitable interest the suit must be dismissed. Local law may determine in whom an interest vests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and equitable owners may be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and equitable owners may be joined as plaintiffs; an equitable title is as good in equity as a legal one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/case law show equity will take jurisdiction where title is doubtful through many assignments; a bill will be dismissed if complainant had no legal or equitable interest (Pelham v. Edelmeyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee retaining any interest must be a party
rubrics_metrics.description: That when the patentee retains any interest in the patent, present or expectant, he must be a party in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee retains any portion of the profits or other interest (present or reversionary/contingent), he should join with his grantee or assignee. Cited cases: Wheeler v. McCormick; Dibble v. Augur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee's standing and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee is entitled to equal recognition with the patentee, even before the agreement to assign has been executed by delivery of the written instrument, provided he has fulfilled the conditions upon which the conveyance was to take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where assignment conditions remain unfulfilled the assignee's right to be a party may be doubted. If an assignment was made before issuance and patent granted to assignee, the applicant/inventor has no interest enforceable in infringement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantee (territorial) may sue for infringements affecting his territory
rubrics_metrics.description: A grantee, within whose territory and against whose exclusive privileges the infringement was committed, may appear as plaintiff whenever the infringement would affect his territorial rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grantees have the same ownership within their territory as patentees/assignees have nationally; they may sue in their own names for infringements within their territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee standing in equity versus at law
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee, although unable to sue in his own name at law, may be a plaintiff in a court of equity if the infringing acts of the defendant impair the value of his license, and may be joined as plaintiff with his licensor, or may sue alone when the licensor himself is the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee to use for one purpose cannot sue without joining the owner of the patent. A licensor may still sue despite having given exclusive license (cases cited). Under certain statutes/license types licensee rights vary (e.g., Sec. 17 act of 1836). A licensor who is the infringer allows licensee to sue alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government lacks standing to sue for infringement pending repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The government, pending proceedings for repeal, has no such interest in the invention or the patent as warrants it in suing for infringement either at law or equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: United States v. Colgate. This is a practical limitation on governmental suits during repeal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of all legal and equitable owners as plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: All legal owners of the patent, and all equitable owners who have been or would be injured by the infringement, should be joined as plaintiffs, and if they refuse to sue as plaintiffs should be made defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties refuse to join they may be made defendants; part-owners may sue alone to protect own interest but must make co-owners respondents. Many cases cited illustrating nuances (e.g., Birdsell v. Shaliol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee's bill not joining owner is demurrable
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill by a licensee not joining the owner of the patent is demurrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cases (Bogart v. Hinds; Birdsell v. Shaliol) show courts require necessary parties to be present in licensee actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: One of multiple licensees may recover without joining others (unless objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of two or more licensees may recover of the infringer his proportion of the profits and damages without joining the others, unless an objection for misjoinder is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no objection is made for nonjoinder, recovery by one licensee may proceed (Adams v. Howard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may order addition of omitted parties during suit
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever necessary parties are omitted at commencement the court may order them to appear and be made parties, and until they do appear it may suspend proceedings and refuse to hear those already on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When licensor sued alone the defendant may obtain order that injured licensee be joined. Additions can be made on motion, at request of party seeking to be added, or by court sua sponte. Order enforceable only if party can be served within jurisdiction or voluntarily appears; cannot add if effect would be to institute a new suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real parties in interest must sue in their own names
rubrics_metrics.description: The real parties in interest must bring their action in equity in their own names and not in that of any attorney or other delegate; corporations must sue in corporate name; unincorporated associations in names of all its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignee should sue in his own name even if assignment not recorded; under Rev. Stat. §4919 an assignee can recover in his own name for past infringements. A suit cannot be brought in the name of an attorney or delegate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misjoinder of plaintiffs — effects and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The misjoinder of plaintiffs who are not real parties in interest can be taken advantage of by defendant on demurrer for want of equity and the bill as to such parties may be dismissed; but misjoinder will not prevent the court from affording equitable relief to any party on the record entitled to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a final decree in the Supreme Court, objection for misjoinder will not avail. Nonjoinder may be cured by adding omitted parties or by disclaimer in favor of actual plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonjoinder may be cured or lead to suspension/dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonjoinder of defendants is no ground of defence unless their presence is necessary to enable the court to decree effectual relief; absence must be pleaded/demurred to and must allege their connection and that they are within the court's jurisdiction; if order to join cannot be enforced the court will stay proceedings or dismiss the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections to nonjoinder are to be taken by demurrer, plea, or answer and set forth what parties are wanting. An amendment creating effectively a new defendant cannot be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveyances pendente lite do not defeat equitable rights of real owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveyances pendente lite do not affect the litigation as between the original plaintiff and defendant, but courts of equity will protect the rights of the real parties and secure to each his due proportion of the damages or profits resulting from the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment of entire interest pending suit may reserve avails for assignor; equity will award avails accordingly while protecting assignee against future infringements by injunction. A conveyance reserving injunction rights calls for no equitable interference because injunction cannot issue for non-owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collusive suits and champerty prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: A collusive action in which one person bears the cost of both parties to obtain a judgment for use against others will not be entertained; agreements to share results or to sue and pay all expenses for part of the proceeds may amount to champerty and are not upheld in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collusive decrees may be annulled on application of a stranger; illustrative cases include Barker v. Todd and Gardner v. Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be defendants in equity for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons who participate in the infringement, whether by performing the infringing act, by ordering it to be committed by their servants, or by directly sharing in its benefits, may be joined as defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations may be sued when they profit by unlawful use and officers who direct employment of infringing devices may be joined. When several distinct individuals are defendants the bill must show how they are related and connected with the same infringing act; where collective operations extend beyond district the bill must allege the defendant's power to direct or prevent the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misjoinder of defendants does not bar relief against guilty parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The misjoinder of defendants does not impair the court's power to afford relief against such of them as are found guilty of the infringement, though the bill as to the others will be dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bill alleges joint or collective and separately wrongful acts, and no objection was made, decree may issue against each defendant separately. Specific procedural rules about amending capacity/adding defendants are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements of a bill in equity for infringement actions (introductory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill in equity in actions for infringement must disclose the substantial groundwork of the case and contain averments (i.e., the claim must set forth the facts and legal basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chunk begins this section and indicates the bill must state the substantive allegations necessary to ground equitable relief; further specifics follow in the treatise beyond this excerpt.
